paragraphs: This paper tests whether neural networks that predict visual brain responses remain accurate when the images change from those used for training. The researchers collected MacaqueITBench, containing neuronal population recordings from the inferior temporal cortex of seven monkeys across 109 sessions. Its more than 300,000 image presentations cover 8,233 unique natural images.

The benchmark separates training and test images using shifts in contrast, hue, intensity, temperature, and saturation. These splits expose weaknesses that conventional evaluation on images from the training distribution can miss. Under some shifts, models retained as little as 20% of their original predictive performance, and their relative rankings changed substantially.

The researchers also found that a simple measure of image similarity strongly predicted performance under these shifts. Specifically, cosine distance between representations from a pretrained object recognition model helped account for neuronal prediction quality. The findings show why evaluating these encoding models across multiple visual distributions can change conclusions about which models best predict brain activity.
neurips-2024-benchmarking-out-of-distrib.tldr: MacaqueITBench reveals substantial accuracy losses and changing model rankings when visual brain-response predictors encounter shifted image distributions.

paragraphs: Zero-shot learning asks a model to recognize classes it did not encounter during training. A further challenge arises when those new classes come from a different distribution than the training classes. This paper examines that problem, using shifts in attributes such as age or gender in person identification as motivating examples.

The authors analyze a setting where the attribute responsible for the shift is unknown beforehand. They show that ordinary training may learn representations that are fragile under such changes. Their algorithm constructs synthetic training environments through hierarchical sampling, then applies an environment balancing penalty intended to encourage representations that work across those environments.

Experiments on simulated and real datasets show improved generalization across diverse class distributions. The contribution is therefore both a model of the problem and a training strategy for addressing it without advance knowledge of the shifting attribute. Its findings emphasize that recognizing unseen classes and handling changes in the distribution of those classes are distinct challenges.
neurips-2024-class-distribution-shifts-i.tldr: Synthetic training environments and environment balancing improve zero-shot representations when unseen classes follow different distributions.

paragraphs: CALDERA compresses a trained language model by replacing each layer's weight matrix with a combination of a quantized matrix and two small, low-rank factors. All three components use low-precision values. This combines two ways of saving memory: reducing the information stored per number and representing part of the matrix through a compact factorization.

The decomposition is chosen to preserve how the original weights act on calibration data. Its optimization objective measures the difference between original and compressed layer outputs on those data, rather than treating every weight error independently. The low-rank factors also support adaptation that can further improve the compressed model's zero-shot performance.

The authors establish theoretical upper bounds on approximation error and study how rank and quantization budgets affect the compression–performance tradeoff. On the evaluated Llama-2 7B, 13B, and 70B models and Llama-3 8B, CALDERA outperforms existing post-training compression methods below 2.5 bits per parameter. This result supports the combined representation specifically in that aggressive compression regime.
neurips-2024-compressing-large-language-.tldr: CALDERA combines quantization with low-rank decomposition to improve tested language models' performance under compression below 2.5 bits per parameter.

paragraphs: This paper studies how diffusion models can generate outputs that satisfy specified constraints and physical principles. The goal includes certifying compliance, so a generated result can be assessed against the requirements imposed on it. This matters for tasks where the desired output must meet explicit mathematical or physical conditions.

The proposed approach reformulates diffusion sampling as a constrained optimization problem. It steers the generated distribution to stay within a specified admissible region. Constraints therefore become part of the generation procedure itself, giving the sampling process a direct way to account for properties that the output is required to possess.

The authors validate the approach on applications involving convex constraints, more challenging non-convex constraints, and ordinary differential equations. Their examples span materials with prescribed shape-related properties, motion informed by physical principles, path optimization, and human motion synthesis. These applications demonstrate the method across several kinds of requirements and output domains. The stated contribution is a framework connecting diffusion generation with explicit constraint satisfaction and certification.
neurips-2024-constrained-synthesis-with-.tldr: The paper reformulates diffusion sampling as constrained optimization to generate outputs that satisfy and certify specified requirements.

paragraphs: Cryo-electron microscopy can reveal three-dimensional biomolecular structures while capturing variation between them. Heterogeneous reconstruction methods try to recover distributions of structures from noisy images without labels identifying the underlying forms. CryoBench addresses the difficulty of comparing these methods when standardized datasets, known answers, and reliable evaluation measures are scarce.

The benchmark contains five datasets with different sources of variation and levels of difficulty. Some represent changes in molecular shape, using designed motions of antibody complexes or samples from a molecular dynamics simulation. Others represent differences in composition, including mixtures of ribosome assembly states and mixtures of 100 common cellular complexes.

The authors evaluate advanced neural and non-neural reconstruction methods, investigate their sensitivity to noise, and introduce quantitative evaluation metrics. This combination makes structural diversity and measurement quality part of the same benchmarking effort. The contribution is an evaluation resource for studying how well reconstruction tools recover heterogeneous structures across controlled challenges, with the intended benefit of supporting further algorithm development.
neurips-2024-cryobench-diverse-and-chall.tldr: CryoBench supplies five diverse datasets and evaluation metrics for comparing methods that reconstruct variable biomolecular structures from cryo-EM images.

paragraphs: A marked point process models a sequence in which events have both occurrence times and labels, called marks. Transformer-based approaches commonly describe these sequences through an intensity function, but generating predictions then relies on the computationally demanding thinning algorithm. This paper changes the modeling arrangement to avoid that inference bottleneck.

The method separates predictions about timing from predictions about event labels. It models the conditional time until the next event with a mixture of log-normal distributions satisfying a Markov property. A Transformer models the conditional probabilities of the marks. This retains attention-based modeling while enabling inference without the thinning procedure used by the compared intensity-based approaches.

The authors report state-of-the-art next-event prediction and experimental advantages for methods that avoid thinning. They also evaluate longer sequences of future predictions, where their method outperforms a baseline designed for that task. Inference takes only a fraction of the time required by the thinning-based baseline, showing a practical benefit alongside the reported predictive gains.
neurips-2024-decomposable-transformer-po.tldr: Separating event timing from Transformer-based label prediction improves reported forecasting performance while avoiding costly thinning-based inference.

paragraphs: Diffusion-based purification aims to defend a model by processing potentially adversarial inputs through a diffusion procedure. This paper investigates whether some of its apparent robustness reflects weaknesses in evaluation. The authors identify two problems: averaging gradients globally can make attacks ineffective, and evaluating a stochastic defense only once can underestimate risks from repeated submissions.

Their attack, DiffHammer, selectively targets vulnerable purification outcomes to work around the gradient problem. It incorporates multiple evaluations into its attack loops and uses a technique called gradient grafting to support efficient, comprehensive evaluation. These components address both how an attack finds a damaging input and how repeated outcomes are considered.

In the reported experiments, DiffHammer produces effective attacks within 10–30 iterations and outperforms other methods. The results challenge confidence in diffusion purification when evaluation accounts for the identified gradient difficulty and resubmission risk. The central implication is that measured robustness depends on whether the evaluation successfully probes the defense's stochastic behavior and vulnerable purification outcomes.
neurips-2024-diffhammer-rethinking-the-r.tldr: DiffHammer exposes weaknesses in diffusion purification by targeting vulnerable outcomes and accounting for repeated evaluations of stochastic defenses.

paragraphs: Electronic health records store information in both structured tables and narrative clinical notes. These formats serve complementary purposes, but their contents can disagree because of human errors or difficult system designs. EHRCon turns checking agreement between them into an explicit dataset and evaluation task, motivated by the patient-safety risks of inconsistent records.

Developed with healthcare professionals using MIMIC-III, the dataset contains manual annotations for 3,943 entities across 105 clinical notes. Those entities were checked against database entries for consistency. The authors provide versions using both the original MIMIC-III schema and the OMOP common data model, broadening the database formats represented by the resource.

The paper also introduces CheckEHR, an eight-stage framework that uses large language models to verify agreement between notes and tables. It reports promising results in both few-shot and zero-shot settings. Together, the dataset and framework establish a concrete way to evaluate automated consistency checking, connecting statements in clinical narratives with corresponding information stored in structured records.
neurips-2024-ehrcon-dataset-for-checking.tldr: EHRCon provides annotated clinical-record consistency checks, and CheckEHR uses language models to compare narrative notes with database tables.

paragraphs: GaussianCut lets a user select an object in a three-dimensional scene by interacting with just one view. The user can supply clicks, rough scribbles, or text. The method operates on scenes represented through 3D Gaussian Splatting, where extracting an object means identifying which of the scene's Gaussians belong to it.

The approach first obtains a rough segmentation using existing two-dimensional image or video segmentation models. It then builds a graph from the scene's Gaussians and defines an energy function that combines scene properties with the user's input. A graph-cut algorithm partitions the Gaussians into foreground and background, refining the initial estimates within the three-dimensional representation.

Evaluations across diverse scenes show that GaussianCut adapts to different scene content and achieves performance competitive with leading 3D segmentation approaches. It does so without additional segmentation-aware training. The contribution is a way to connect simple interaction in one view with object selection across views, using graph optimization to refine existing segmentation predictions.
neurips-2024-gaussiancut-interactive-seg.tldr: GaussianCut combines single-view user input, existing segmentation models, and graph cuts to extract objects from 3D Gaussian scenes.

paragraphs: The k-center problem with outliers covers a set of points using at most k balls while allowing up to z points to remain uncovered. Its objective is to minimize the largest ball radius. This paper studies the fully dynamic setting, where points can be inserted and deleted and the clustering must be maintained as those updates occur.

The proposed algorithm gives a 4 + epsilon approximation to the radius while allowing up to (1 + epsilon)z uncovered points. Its guarantee is probabilistic, with the stated success probability of 1 − k/e^{Omega(log k)}. The extra allowance for outliers is part of the guarantee and accompanies the improved radius approximation.

The algorithm applies to general metric spaces and provides an expected amortized update-time bound, measuring update cost on average over a sequence rather than promising the same cost for every update. It improves the radius factor over the cited 14 + epsilon dynamic algorithm. The result strengthens the available quality guarantee for maintaining approximate clusters while the underlying point set changes.
neurips-2024-improved-guarantees-for-ful.tldr: A dynamic clustering algorithm improves the radius approximation to 4 + epsilon while permitting a small multiplicative increase in outliers.

paragraphs: Adversarial training and robustness distillation can improve resistance to adversarial examples, yet that protection may be uneven across classes. A model can defend some classes well while remaining vulnerable on others. This paper studies that class-level disparity, including when a smaller student learns from a larger teacher through knowledge distillation.

The authors connect this disparity to the smoothness of the teacher's soft labels: how concentrated or spread out the assigned probabilities are. They support the connection with empirical observations and theoretical analysis. Their Anti-Bias Soft Label Distillation method adjusts this smoothness separately for different classes by assigning class-specific distillation temperatures during training.

These adjustments adaptively aim to reduce gaps in the student's error risk across classes. In extensive experiments, the method outperforms compared adversarial training, robustness distillation, and robust fairness approaches on Normalized Standard Deviation, the paper's combined measure of robustness and fairness. The result supports class-dependent soft-label control as a mechanism for improving the balance of adversarial protection.
neurips-2024-improving-adversarial-robus.tldr: Class-specific distillation temperatures improve the reported balance of adversarial robustness across easy and hard classes.

paragraphs: Distributed optimization requires a server and multiple workers to exchange information as they solve an optimization problem. This paper studies how to reduce that communication for nonconvex optimization under function similarity. It begins with a simplified setting where worker-to-server costs are negligible, allowing the analysis to focus on messages sent from the server.

The proposed MARINA-P method compresses those outgoing messages using a collection of correlated compressors. With permutation compressors, its theoretical server-to-worker communication complexity improves as the number of workers grows. The analysis establishes an advantage over existing algorithms in the considered setting, making worker count part of the communication benefit.

The authors then build M3 by combining MARINA-P with compression in the opposite direction and a momentum step. M3 provides provable improvements in total communication complexity as more workers participate. Experiments closely match the theoretical findings. Together, the methods address both an isolated downlink bottleneck and the broader case where communication in both directions matters.
neurips-2024-improving-the-worst-case-bi.tldr: MARINA-P and M3 provide communication guarantees that improve with worker count for downlink and bidirectional distributed optimization.

paragraphs: Causal Bayesian networks describe relationships among variables, but calculating probabilities for statements involving interventions can be difficult. This paper examines when such probabilities can be uniquely estimated. Its scope includes probabilities of sufficiency and necessity, which concern whether a cause can produce an outcome or was needed for it.

The authors show that relatively simple independence assumptions can make these estimates unique. They describe the assumptions as often realistic and discuss circumstances in which they are appropriate. These assumptions are a substantive part of the result: the claimed ability to determine intervention-related probabilities depends on their suitability for the problem being studied.

In many cases of interest, when those assumptions hold appropriately, the resulting estimates can be evaluated from observational data. This offers a route to answering certain causal questions in settings where experiments are impractical or impossible. The contribution is therefore a conditional identification result, connecting explicit assumptions about independence to the possibility of calculating otherwise challenging intervention probabilities.
neurips-2024-intervention-and-conditioni.tldr: Appropriate independence assumptions can uniquely determine intervention probabilities, with observational data sufficient to evaluate them in many cases.

paragraphs: MMBench-Video evaluates how well large vision-language models understand lengthy videos containing multiple shots. The paper argues that existing video question-answering benchmarks do not adequately cover video content or assess temporal understanding. Its benchmark uses long YouTube videos and free-form questions to create an evaluation closer to practical video-understanding tasks.

The questions are human-annotated according to a deliberately constructed taxonomy of abilities, with particular attention to temporal reasoning. This organizes the benchmark around the skills being tested, rather than relying solely on an overall question-answering score. The free-form format allows models to produce answers without choosing from a fixed list.

The authors use GPT-4 for automated assessment and report greater accuracy and robustness than earlier language-model-based evaluation approaches. They evaluate both proprietary and open-source vision-language models, including models for images and videos. The contribution combines an evaluation dataset, an ability structure, and an assessment procedure to make broader video comprehension more systematically measurable.
neurips-2024-mmbench-video-a-long-form-m.tldr: MMBench-Video tests long-video understanding and temporal reasoning through human-annotated free-form questions and automated assessment.

paragraphs: The Latent Prompt Transformer treats molecule design as generation conditioned on desired biological properties or chemical constraints. It connects those requirements to molecule generation through a latent vector. That vector serves as a prompt for a causal Transformer and also supplies the information used by a property-prediction model.

A third component learns a distribution over latent prompts by transforming Gaussian noise. The system is initially trained on molecule–property pairs using maximum likelihood. During optimization, posterior sampling infers prompts consistent with target properties and constraints, and the Transformer uses those prompts to generate molecules autoregressively, building their representation one step at a time.

After initial training, an online learning procedure progressively moves the model's distribution toward regions supporting the desired properties. Experiments report effective discovery of useful molecules in single-objective, multi-objective, and structure-constrained tasks, together with strong sample efficiency. The approach therefore combines a shared latent representation for generation and property prediction with continued learning directed toward the design objective.
neurips-2024-molecule-design-by-latent-p.tldr: The Latent Prompt Transformer uses property-conditioned latent prompts and online learning to guide efficient molecular design.

paragraphs: Low-rank approximation compresses a dataset into a lower-dimensional representation, while column subset selection represents it using selected original columns. This paper studies socially fair versions of both problems, where approximation quality is evaluated across the data's subpopulations. The objective makes group-level loss central to the representation being chosen.

The authors establish a computational obstacle: under certain standard complexity hypotheses, even achieving a constant-factor approximation for fair low-rank approximation requires exponential time. They also provide an improved algorithm when the number of groups and the desired approximation factor are constant. Its stated dependence changes from the naive n^{poly(k)} to 2^{poly(k)}, benefiting settings with many observations n.

Finally, the paper gives polynomial-time bicriteria approximation algorithms for both fair low-rank approximation and fair column subset selection. Bicriteria guarantees permit a tradeoff across criteria, so they offer a different guarantee from the hardness result's target. Together, these results map both computational barriers and available algorithmic routes for incorporating subpopulation loss into data compression.
neurips-2024-on-socially-fair-low-rank-a.tldr: The paper establishes conditional hardness for fair low-rank approximation while providing faster restricted-setting and polynomial-time bicriteria algorithms.

paragraphs: This paper investigates why general pretraining can leave language models weak on specialized tasks even when relevant knowledge appears in the training corpus. The authors identify rare, unevenly distributed domain information as a leading cause. Their neural tangent kernel analysis indicates that such long-tail examples are commonly overlooked during gradient updates and consequently memorized poorly.

They propose a Cluster-guided Sparse Expert layer that groups semantically related information and assigns extra experts to long-tail knowledge during pretraining. The design relies on the intuition that similar meanings lie close together in embedding space. It is lightweight enough to be added to only several deep layers of the model.

During training, the authors observe long-tail knowledge forming isolated outlier clusters, especially in deeper representations. Their experiments find that CSE-based models pretrained this way outperform regularly pretrained-and-finetuned models on various downstream tasks. These results suggest a route to reducing the need for a separate domain-specific pretraining stage by better learning rare domain knowledge during initial pretraining.
neurips-2024-once-read-is-enough-domain-.tldr: Cluster-guided sparse experts help language models learn rare domain knowledge during initial pretraining, suggesting less need for separate domain-specific pretraining.

paragraphs: Questions with many possible answers can expose a language model's knowledge boundary differently from questions with one concrete answer. A model may know some valid responses while producing uncertain or incorrect others. This paper therefore probes individual ambiguous answers to semi-open-ended questions instead of treating each whole question as simply answerable or unanswerable.

The method constructs questions with a language model and gathers responses from a target model. Because black-box output probabilities are unavailable, an open-source auxiliary model helps explore less obvious answers. Semantic representations support probability estimates for existing answers, and their generation probabilities are reduced to encourage broader exploration. Retrieval-augmented evaluation and the target's self-evaluation then support four categories of ambiguous answers.

Using this process, the authors build a dataset probing GPT-4. They find poor performance on semi-open-ended questions and frequent failure to recognize its own knowledge boundary. The auxiliary LLaMA-2-13B model discovers both correct answers GPT-4 overlooked and misleading wrong answers it struggles to reject, revealing weaknesses that question-level answerability checks can miss.
neurips-2024-perception-of-knowledge-bou.tldr: Exploring ambiguous answers to semi-open-ended questions reveals gaps in GPT-4's knowledge and awareness of those gaps.

paragraphs: PrivacyLens evaluates whether language-model agents respect privacy norms while carrying out communication tasks. Privacy-sensitive situations depend heavily on context and include many uncommon cases, making them difficult to cover with simple tests. The framework starts from privacy-sensitive seeds and expands them into richer scenarios and sequences of agent actions.

The authors build the dataset from privacy norms grounded in research literature and crowdsourced seeds. Its multiple evaluation levels allow comparison between what a model says about a situation and what it does while following user instructions. This distinction matters because answering a privacy question correctly does not necessarily predict appropriate behavior during an agent task.

The evaluation finds a discrepancy between probing-question performance and actual actions. GPT-4 and Llama-3-70B leak sensitive information in 25.68% and 38.69% of tested cases, respectively, even with privacy-enhancing instructions. The authors also expand individual seeds into multiple trajectories for red-teaming, showing how the framework can generate varied tests of privacy leakage risk.
neurips-2024-privacylens-evaluating-priv.tldr: PrivacyLens finds that language models' stated privacy awareness can diverge from sensitive-information leakage during agent actions.

paragraphs: QUEST addresses the problem of generating several translations that are both good and meaningfully varied. Translation-model likelihood can correlate poorly with translation quality, while evaluation metrics such as COMET and BLEURT align better with human judgments. However, selecting a single answer with a very high metric score risks exploiting noise in that quality estimate.

The method uses estimated quality to define the energy of a Gibbs distribution over translations. It then applies Metropolis-Hastings sampling to draw multiple outputs from high-density regions. This turns quality estimates into guidance for sampling a collection of translations, rather than concentrating the entire decision on one estimated optimum.

Experiments use Alma-7b and Tower-7b for translation between English and German and between English and Russian, in both directions. The reported results show high-quality, diverse outputs across these settings. The approach's significance is its direct treatment of quality and diversity as a sampling problem, intended to reduce excessive dependence on any single noisy quality score.
neurips-2024-quest-quality-aware-metropo.tldr: QUEST samples from a quality-guided distribution to produce diverse, high-quality translations without relying on one maximum-scoring output.

paragraphs: Unsupervised graph domain adaptation transfers knowledge from a graph with many labels to a target graph without labels. Differences between the graphs can make that transfer difficult. This paper introduces GDABench to address the lack of standardized experimental settings and fair comparisons, bringing 16 algorithms together across a range of adaptation tasks.

The experiments show that existing methods' performance varies considerably between datasets and transfer scenarios. The authors particularly emphasize graph structural shifts when source and target distributions differ substantially. Their findings point to the way relationships between nodes change as an important consideration for designing effective adaptation strategies.

The study also finds that simple graph neural network variants can surpass leading adaptation baselines when they use suitable neighborhood aggregation mechanisms. This highlights the importance of how information from connected nodes is combined. The accompanying PyGDA library standardizes training and evaluation of existing methods, supporting reproducibility and making it easier to investigate which approaches work under particular graph shifts.
neurips-2024-revisiting-benchmarking-and.tldr: GDABench shows that graph adaptation performance depends strongly on the scenario, with structural shifts and neighborhood aggregation playing important roles.

paragraphs: RGB-event single-object tracking combines conventional image data with event data to follow one target. This paper argues that existing approaches emphasize complementary appearance information while underusing event-stream motion for distinguishing targets from distractors over time. It adopts a multi-object tracking perspective, tracking distractors alongside the intended target to improve robustness.

An appearance model first proposes candidates. Initial tracking predictions and RGB-event features are then encoded into appearance and motion embeddings. A spatial-temporal Transformer encoder uses those embeddings to learn relationships across space and time and produce features that help distinguish the candidates from one another.

A dual-branch Transformer decoder uses both appearance and motion information to match candidates, supporting the decision about which candidate is the target. Across the multiple benchmark datasets evaluated, the method achieves state-of-the-art performance on every tested dataset. The findings support treating competing objects as part of the tracking problem and explicitly using motion to resolve associations, rather than relying primarily on candidate appearance.
neurips-2024-revisiting-motion-informati.tldr: Tracking distractors alongside the target and combining motion with appearance improves RGB-event tracking across all evaluated benchmarks.

paragraphs: Generalized-linear dynamical models are used to describe time series such as neuronal spikes and categorical decisions. Many applications need to model two sources together while distinguishing dynamics they share from dynamics specific to each. This paper develops a learning procedure for that separation, which most existing variants and learning algorithms do not support.

The proposed method uses a multi-step analytical subspace identification algorithm to learn a model with explicit shared and private dynamics. Simulations demonstrate its ability to disentangle the two sources while being agnostic to their respective observation distributions. The authors also apply it to two neural-data settings involving population spiking activity and a secondary time series.

On both synthetic and real data, the learned models decode one time series from the other more accurately than models learned with existing algorithms. They achieve this using lower-dimensional latent states. These findings support the value of explicitly separating shared from private dynamics when the objective includes predicting the relationship between two observed processes.
neurips-2024-spectral-learning-of-shared.tldr: A subspace identification algorithm separates shared and private dynamics between two time series and improves cross-series decoding with smaller latent states.

paragraphs: This paper studies Thompson Sampling in linear combinatorial semi-bandits, where decisions involve combinations of components and feedback reveals component-level rewards. It works under a subgaussian reward assumption. The central question is how the method's regret, measuring the cost of learning while making decisions, grows with the dimension of the problem.

The authors propose what they identify as the first Thompson Sampling method whose finite-time regret avoids exponential scaling with dimension in this setting. This is a guarantee about performance over a finite learning horizon. It addresses a potentially severe dependence on problem size in the analysis of combinatorial Thompson Sampling.

The paper also establishes a mismatched sampling paradox. A learner that knows the reward distributions and samples from the correct posterior can perform exponentially worse than one using a carefully chosen Gaussian posterior without that knowledge. The comparison shows that correct posterior sampling can be disadvantageous in the demonstrated setting; it does not claim that every mismatched posterior is better.
neurips-2024-thompson-sampling-for-combi.tldr: A Thompson Sampling method avoids exponential dimension dependence in regret, while a paradox shows that correct posterior sampling can perform exponentially worse.

paragraphs: Partial-label learning trains a classifier when each example comes with a set of candidate labels. Modern methods have become increasingly complex by borrowing techniques from other areas. This paper empirically investigates which ingredients actually address label ambiguity, aiming to extract simple design principles from the behavior of successful approaches.

The analysis finds that strong accuracy on benchmarks with simulated partial labels can overstate the value of some general techniques. Those techniques may improve learned representations while contributing relatively little to resolving the candidate-label problem itself. Across successful methods, the authors identify a common progression from uniform pseudo-label probabilities toward a single selected label.

The study highlights mini-batch partial-label purification as critical to top performance in its analysis. Guided by these findings, the authors introduce a minimal working algorithm that is simple yet effective, together with an improved strategy for implementing their design principles. The contribution clarifies the distinction between learning better features and progressively resolving ambiguous supervision.
neurips-2024-what-makes-partial-label-le.tldr: An empirical analysis links effective partial-label learning to progressive pseudo-label purification and derives a simple working algorithm.
